finding.claim: Unauthenticated POST to /settings/email reaches set_email with g.uid=None because the route uses login_optional, which never aborts; no identity or ownership check on the account being modified.
finding.source: Anonymous HTTP POST to /settings/email (no session required)
finding.sink: set_email(g.uid, "new@example.org") at routes.py:37 — protected account-email change

trace.note: g.uid = session.get('uid') -> None for anonymous request; no abort

finding.guards_checked: login_optional performs no abort (routes.py:19-25); no ownership/identity check on target account; no CSRF token. Sibling change_password uses login_required, suggesting decorator mismatch. Impact depends on set_email (stub at routes.py:48-49): if None acts as a wildcard in an UPDATE, impact is mass modification; hardcoded example.org limits direct email-reset takeover.

verdict.guard_found: none. login_optional (routes.py:19-25) sets g.uid = session.get("uid") (None when anonymous) and never aborts. The route at routes.py:34-38 is decorated with @login_optional, not @login_required. change_email has no identity or ownership check before calling set_email(g.uid, ...) at routes.py:37. The return value of set_email is unused, but that does not matter because the call happens regardless. No CSRF protection is present in this file.
verdict.reason: The anonymous POST to /settings/email reaches the change_email handler, which calls set_email(None, "new@example.org") at routes.py:37 because login_optional at routes.py:22-23 never aborts, while the sibling /settings/password route at routes.py:42 uses login_required. The impact is conditional, since set_email at routes.py:48-49 is a stub (`pass`), so the account-modification effect is inferred from its name rather than shown in this file.

finding.claim: POST /settings/password sets the account password to the hardcoded constant 'hunter2' with no current-password, re-auth, or MFA check; the password is a hardcoded credential in source.
finding.source: Any valid session (stolen cookie, or cross-site request carrying the victim's cookie per F3)

trace.note: set_password stub (pass); real impact depends on implementation

finding.guards_checked: login_required (routes.py:8-16) verifies session presence only; no current-password check, no re-auth/MFA, no CSRF protection; password is not user-supplied. Hardcoded credential violates org policy and should be flagged to Security.

verdict.guard_found: login_required (routes.py:8-16) only checks that "uid" is in the session (line 11), and the password is a constant at call site routes.py:44 with no current-password, re-auth, or MFA check; no effective control blocks it. Caveat: set_password (routes.py:52-53) is a no-op stub, so no password change actually happens in this repo.
verdict.reason: Every trace line matches routes.py:41-52: any holder of a valid session can reach the POST /settings/password route (routes.py:41-45), which passes the hardcoded constant "hunter2" to set_password (routes.py:44) with no re-authentication, so the hardcoded credential and missing re-auth flaw is real, but the account-takeover impact depends on a real set_password implementation that is not present here.

finding.claim: Cookie-authenticated state-changing POST routes (/settings/email, /settings/password) have no CSRF protection; exploitability depends on SameSite cookie configuration not present in this file.
finding.source: Cross-site page causing victim browser to POST with session cookie (or same-site subdomain attacker)

trace.note: Session cookie is the sole credential (also routes.py:22)

finding.guards_checked: No CSRF token in these routes. SESSION_COOKIE_SAMESITE / session cookie settings not in repo; Flask default leaves SameSite unset, and browsers defaulting to Lax block cross-site POST, but same-site subdomain attacks are not blocked by Lax. Config unverified.

verdict.guard_found: No CSRF token or Origin/Referer check on either route (routes.py:34-45). The only session logic is login_required (routes.py:11-13) and login_optional (routes.py:22), which authenticate but do not protect against forged requests. SameSite cookie settings are not in the repo, so browser-enforced SameSite is unverified.
verdict.reason: The missing CSRF check is confirmed at routes.py:34-45 and the trace lines are accurate, but whether a cross-site attacker can forge the POST depends on SESSION_COOKIE_SAMESITE, which is set outside this file (Flask leaves it unset, so browsers default to Lax, which blocks cross-site POSTs but not same-site ones). Also, set_email and set_password at routes.py:48-53 are stubs with hardcoded values, so the real impact cannot be assessed from this file.
